questions.stem: What does Le Chatelier's principle state?

options.text: Reactions always reach equilibrium within one minute
If conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change and partially restore the original conditions
Catalysts always shift the position of equilibrium to the right
Increasing temperature always increases the yield of products

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium will shift to counteract (oppose) that change.

questions.stem: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what happens to the position of equilibrium if the pressure is increased?

options.text: It shifts to the left, producing more N₂ and H₂
It shifts to the right, producing more NH₃
It does not change
The reaction stops completely

questions.explanation: Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 + 3) while the right has 2 moles, so equilibrium shifts right, producing more ammonia.

questions.stem: If the forward reaction is exothermic, what effect does increasing the temperature have on the equilibrium position?

options.text: Equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing product yield
Equilibrium shifts to the left, decreasing product yield
No effect on the equilibrium position
The reaction becomes irreversible

questions.explanation: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction to absorb the extra heat. If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse (endothermic) reaction is favoured, shifting equilibrium to the left.

questions.stem: What is the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium?

options.text: It shifts equilibrium to the right
It shifts equilibrium to the left
It does not change the position of equilibrium, but equilibrium is reached faster
It prevents equilibrium from being reached

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium. It simply allows equilibrium to be reached more quickly.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), if the concentration of A is increased, what happens?

options.text: The equilibrium shifts to the left
The equilibrium shifts to the right to use up the extra A
The equilibrium position does not change
The concentration of B also increases

questions.explanation: Increasing the concentration of reactant A causes the equilibrium to shift to the right to use up the extra A, producing more product C. This is in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle.

questions.stem: In the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), what happens to the equilibrium position if pressure is decreased?

options.text: Equilibrium shifts to the right (fewer moles of gas)
Equilibrium shifts to the left (more moles of gas)
No change occurs
The reaction becomes irreversible

questions.explanation: Decreasing pressure favours the side with more moles of gas. The left side has 3 moles of gas (2 + 1) while the right has 2, so equilibrium shifts to the left.

questions.stem: For an endothermic forward reaction at equilibrium, which change would increase the yield of products?

options.text: Decreasing the temperature
Increasing the temperature
Adding a catalyst
Removing some reactants

questions.explanation: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. If the forward reaction is endothermic, higher temperature shifts equilibrium to the right, increasing product yield.
